# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Thank goodness, studying or instructing geometry is behind me,” remarked Nell Harcourt, rather vengefully, while she slammed a slightly worn copy of Euclid into a large book chest, struck the cover closed victoriously, and perched on it, gazing at Isolde Duckett across the Grey Shutters attic, with morning-sky-like gray eyes.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0000 }

A shadowy, suggestive, and delightful place was the garret, just as every garret ought to be. Sitting beside the open window, Nell felt the sweet, scented, sun-warm air of the August afternoon blow past; outdoors, poplar boughs were rustling and tossing in the wind; further off lay the woods, through which Linger Lane snaked its enchanted path, along with the old apple orchard that continued to yield its rosy harvests generously. Moreover, towering above everything in the blue southern sky was a vast mountain range of snowy clouds. Looking out the opposite window revealed a view of a far-off, white-capped, blue sea—the lovely St. Lawrence Gulf, where Abegweit floats like a jewel, though its softer, sweeter Indian name was abandoned long ago for the more prosaic title of St. Brendan’s Island.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0001 }

Having aged three years since our previous encounter, Isolde Duckett was now rather matronly. Nevertheless, her eyes retained their blackness and brilliance, her cheeks their rosiness, and her dimples their enchantment, just as they were during those past days when an oath of everlasting friendship was sworn by her and Nell Harcourt within the Pear Hill garden. Nestled in her arms was a tiny, slumbering child with black curls, who throughout two joyful years had been called “Small Nell Lucinda” by the Brierley community. Naturally, the residents of Brierley understood the reason Isolde gave her the name Nell, yet those same Brierley residents felt confused regarding the Lucinda. No individual named Lucinda had ever existed within the Pembroke or Duckett families. It was suggested by Mrs. Gorham Pullen that Isolde had likely discovered the moniker inside a cheap book, while she expressed surprise that Gideon lacked the wisdom to forbid it. Isolde and Nell, however, exchanged a smile. The origin of Small Nell Lucinda’s name was something only they understood.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0002 }

“It was always geometry that you disliked,” Isolde remarked, smiling in recollection. “Anyhow, I would imagine you must be truly pleased to have finished with teaching.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0003 }

“Oh, geometry aside, I have constantly enjoyed instruction. My previous three years spent in Eastmere were quite agreeable. Upon my return, Mrs. Gorham Pullen informed me of the unlikelihood that I would consider matrimony so much superior to teaching as I anticipated. Mrs. Gorham obviously shares Hamlet’s view that enduring our present troubles might be preferable to rushing toward unfamiliar ones.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0004 }

A laugh from Nell—just as cheerful and captivating as in past times, though now carrying a new tone of gentleness and adulthood—echoed across the attic room. Downstairs in the kitchen, Thirza was preparing blue plum preserve when the sound reached her, bringing a smile to her face; she then sighed upon reflecting that the future would rarely hear that cherished laughter reverberating inside Grey Shutters. The realization that Nell intended to wed Hugh Carrow had brought Thirza greater delight than any other event in her existence; yet every delight inevitably casts its own small shadow of sadness. Throughout those three years spent in Eastmere, Nell had frequently returned home to stay for breaks and weekends; however, following this event, one could expect nothing more than a twice-yearly stay.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0005 }

“What Mrs. Gorham says doesn’t need to worry you,” Isolde said, possessing the peaceful confidence of a woman married for four years. “Naturally, there are ups and downs in married life. Expecting all things to proceed smoothly all the time is a mistake. However, Nell, I can give you my assurance that life is happy, provided your husband is the right man.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0006 }

Nell hid a smile. The grand, experienced manner that Isolde put on had always brought her a bit of amusement.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0007 }

“It is likely I will be wearing them as well, once four years of marriage have passed for me,” occurred to her. “However, my sense of humor will undoubtedly save me from that.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0008 }

“Has the location of your future home been decided yet?” inquired Isolde, holding Small Nell Lucinda close with that matchless maternal touch that perpetually caused a sensation—partly unalloyed delight and partly an unusual, otherworldly ache—to course through the heart of Nell, which was laden with tender, unspoken aspirations and longings.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0009 }

“Indeed. I intended to inform you of that when I rang you to travel down here today. Incidentally, I am unable to grasp that telephones are actually present in Brierley at this moment. For this sweet, unhurried ancient location, it seems so absurdly current and contemporary.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0010 }

“The A. V. I. S. deserves our gratitude for those,” Isolde remarked. “Had they not embraced the issue and driven it to completion, we would not have secured the line. So much discouragement was aimed at them that it would have dampened any organization. Even so, they persevered. Nell, establishing that society was a magnificent service to Brierley. The fun we experienced during our gatherings was unforgettable! Is the blue hall, along with Judson Tibbs’s plan to put medicine ads on his fence, something you will ever erase from your memory?”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0011 }

“I am not entirely sure of my gratitude toward the A. V. I. S. regarding the telephone,” Nell remarked. “Certainly, it is extremely useful—surpassing even our previous method of communicating through candlelight signals! Furthermore, as Mrs. Agatha notes, 'Brierley must keep up with the procession, that’s what.’ Yet I possess a lingering feeling against Brierley being ruined by the things Mr. Pettifer terms 'modern inconveniences’ when attempting humor. My desire would be to preserve it perpetually as it existed during those beloved past times. Such a wish is foolish—and sentimental—and impossible. Consequently, I will turn wise, practical, and possible without delay. The telephone, by Mr. Pettifer’s admission, represents 'a buster of a good thing’—notwithstanding the awareness that roughly six curious individuals are likely overhearing everything on the circuit.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0012 }

“That’s the most dreadful part,” Isolde uttered with a sigh. “Hearing the earpieces being replaced every time you make a call is terribly irritating. People claim that Mrs. Gorham Pullen demanded her ’phone be placed inside their kitchen for the sole purpose of eavesdropping every time it chimed while simultaneously watching over the meal. Earlier today, upon your call to me, the chiming of that strange Tulk clock reached my ears clearly. Consequently, Flossie or Tibby was undoubtedly eavesdropping.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0013 }

“Ah, that explains your remark, ‘You’ve got a new clock at Grey Shutters, haven’t you?’ Your meaning completely escaped me. The moment you finished speaking, a sharp click reached my ears. The Tulk receiver was being slammed down with cursed force, I presume. Regardless, let us forget about the Tulks. To quote Mrs. Agatha, ‘Tulks they always were and Tulks they always will be, world without end, amen.’ My desire is to discuss more agreeable subjects. The location of my future residence has been fully decided.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0014 }

“Oh, Nell, where? Near here is where I truly hope it is.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0015 }

“No-o-o, the disadvantage lies right there. Hugh intends to make his home in Seven Gulls Harbor, which is sixty miles away.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0016 }

“Sixty! It could just as easily be six hundred,” Isolde sighed. “Now, I am never able to travel any farther from home than Port Marlow.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0017 }

“You must visit Seven Gulls. On the Island, no harbor surpasses its beauty. At its head lies a small settlement named Glen St. Agnes, where Dr. David Carrow has been a practitioner for half a century. As you are aware, he is the great-uncle of Hugh. Upon his retirement, Hugh will assume his medical practice. Since Dr. Carrow intends to remain in his home, however, we must secure a residence of our own. Although its true identity and location remain unknown to me for now, my imagination has fully appointed a modest house o’dreams—a small, enchanting castle in Spain.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0018 }

“To what location will you travel for your honeymoon?” Isolde inquired.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0019 }

“To no place at all. Please do not appear shocked, dearest Isolde. You propose Mrs. Gorham Pullen. Unquestionably, she will patronizingly observe that individuals unable to pay for wedding 'towers’ show genuine good sense by foregoing them; subsequently, she will prompt my memory that Odette traveled to Europe for her own. It is my desire to pass MY honeymoon at Seven Gulls inside my very own cherished dream house.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0020 }

“And you have chosen to forgo having a bridesmaid?”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0021 }

“No candidates are available. Regarding matrimony, you, Cressy, Honora, and Odette got ahead of me; meanwhile, Mabel works as a teacher in Vancouver. I do not possess any additional 'kindred soul' and refuse to accept a bridesmaid who lacks that qualification.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0022 }

“Isolde asked anxiously, “Will you not be wearing a veil, though?””
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0023 }

“Indeed, that's true. Without one, I would not feel like a bride. I recall saying to Obed, on that night when he escorted me to Grey Shutters, that my expectations of becoming a bride were non-existent because my appearance was so plain that nobody would ever desire to take me as a wife—except perhaps a foreign missionary. At that time, I believed that foreign missionaries could not be picky about appearances if they needed a woman to jeopardize her life amid cannibals. You ought to have beheld the foreign missionary who married Honora. He possessed the good looks and mystery of those fantasies we once intended to wed ourselves, Isolde; no man I ever encountered was better dressed, and he gushed about Honora’s 'ethereal, golden beauty.’ Naturally, though, Japan has no cannibals.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0024 }

“At any rate, your bridal gown is heavenly,” Isolde uttered with a sigh of delight. “Being so tall and slight, you will resemble a complete queen wearing it. Nell, in what manner DO you remain so thin? My weight has increased even more—before long, my waist will completely disappear.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0025 }

“Being heavy or thin appears to be predetermined,” Nell remarked. “In any case, the comment Mrs. Gorham Pullen made to me upon my return from Eastmere, 'Well, Nell, you’re just about as skinny as ever,’ cannot be directed at you. Calling someone 'slender’ conveys a certain romance, whereas 'skinny’ carries a distinctly altered flavor.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0026 }

“Mrs. Gorham was speaking regarding your trousseau. It is as lovely as Odette’s, she acknowledges, even though she remarks that Odette wed a millionaire while you are merely marrying a 'poor young doctor without a cent to his name.'”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0027 }

A laugh came from Nell.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0028 }

“My gowns ARE lovely. Pretty items are things I adore. The initial attractive frock I possessed comes to mind—the brown gloria provided to me by Obed for our school performance. Up until then, all my possessions were terribly unattractive. That evening, it felt as though I entered a different realm.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0029 }

“During that evening, Hugh performed 'Bingen on the Rhine,' turning his gaze toward you as he uttered, 'There’s another, NOT a sister.’ Furthermore, you felt such intense rage when he placed your pink tissue rose into his breast pocket! Back at that time, you hardly envisioned that he would one day become your husband.”
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0030 }

“Oh, well, another case of predestination is right there,” Nell laughed, while they walked down the stairs from the garret.
{: #nw-v04-c01-p0031 }
